title: Connect and Schedule the Beacon Automation
subtitle: Configure how it connects, what starts it, and what happens when it breaks
scenario: You have built the whole payment run workflow. None of it runs by itself yet. Before anyone can rely on it, the automation needs a connection to ap shared mailbox, an identity to run as, something to start it, and a decision about what happens when a step fails. That configuration is the difference between a design and a system.
input:
IT setup sheet - Beacon automation account

Source system: AP shared mailbox (team-owned). Also available: Your personal inbox, The controller's desktop folder.
Identity: service account, provisioned for this automation.
Secret: the raw token is xoxb-4471-9920-QpLm2Vt8Zr - it is ALSO registered in the vault as vault://beacon/ap-mailbox.
- Check interval: the desk wants it between 10 and 30 minutes.
Retry guidance: three attempts, then stop.
Failure guidance: park the run where it can be found and notify the on-call owner.
instructions: Choose the system the automation connects to, and the identity it runs as.
Point the secret at its vault reference - do not paste the token itself.
Set what starts a run, and how often it checks.
Set the retry count and what happens after the retries are used up.

fields.label: System
fields.explain: The automation must not depend on one person's account. It connects to the ap shared mailbox the team owns, so it keeps working when someone leaves.

fields.label: Auth method
options: A shared password in the flow
fields.explain: A flow authenticated as a person breaks the day that person changes their password or leaves. It runs as a service account with its own identity.

fields.label: Secret
fields.explain: Store a REFERENCE to the secret, never the value. A pasted token lives in the flow definition, in every export, and in the run history - forever, and for everyone who can read them.

fields.label: Trigger mode
fields.explain: Vendors email invoices; the mailbox cannot notify you. The automation checks on a timer. A webhook would need every vendor to integrate, which they will not.

fields.label: Check every (min)
fields.explain: Invoices arrive all morning and the run closes at 3:00 PM. Checking more often than every 10 minutes wastes mailbox quota; less often than 30 risks missing the cutoff.

fields.label: Retries
fields.explain: Three retries clears a transient blip without hammering a system that is genuinely down. Zero gives up on a hiccup; ten turns an outage into an attack.

fields.label: Then
fields.explain: A failure nobody sees is the worst outcome available. Park the run where it can be found and tell a person.

copilotPrompt: Explain the difference between polling and a webhook trigger, and why an automation should reference a secret from a vault instead of storing the value. Keep it to a few sentences.
successMessage: Connector configured. The automation can now run on its own.

intro.heading: Before you build: the automation is a system too

sections.title: What this record does
sections.body: The connector config is how the payment run workflow stops being a design and starts being something that runs at 8:30 AM whether or not anyone is watching. (Domain note: a CONNECTOR is the piece that lets the automation talk to another system. A CREDENTIAL is what proves it is allowed to. A TRIGGER is what starts a run - either the automation POLLS (checks on a timer) or the source sends a WEBHOOK (pushes the moment something happens). A RUN is one execution. A RETRY is running a failed step again.)

sections.title: Why the identity matters
sections.body: An automation authenticated as a person inherits that person's access and dies with their password. A service account has its own identity, its own least-privilege permissions, and an owner who is not a single human being.

sections.title: Why a reference, not a value
sections.body: A pasted secret is in the flow definition, in every export of it, in source control if the flow is versioned, and often in the run history. A reference resolves at run time and can be rotated without touching the automation.

sections.title: Why failure behavior is a design decision
sections.body: Every automation fails eventually. The question the config answers is what happens next: retried, parked where someone will see it, or silently dropped. Only one of those is acceptable.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You would open the flow's connections, note what identity it runs as, set the trigger and its interval, add a retry policy and a failure path, then run it once and read the run.

bestFit.how: a connection reference owned by the AP service account, not a personal connection
the scenario's Connections, with the secret held by the connection rather than a field
a vault-backed secret and a client that refuses to start without it

takeaway.heading: Automation connected
takeaway.before: The payment run workflow was a design that only ran when a person ran it.
takeaway.after: The automation has a governed connection, a trigger, and a defined failure path.
takeaway.capability: The workflow can now run on a trigger, as a governed identity, with a defined failure path.
takeaway.auditNote: The config names the identity, the secret reference, and the failure path, so an auditor can answer 'what runs this, as whom, and what happens when it breaks' without reading the flow.
points: You created connector-config.json, the record of how this automation connects and runs.
The secret is referenced, not stored, so it can be rotated without touching the automation.
The workflow can now run on a trigger, as a governed identity, with a defined failure path.
